﴿يَغْفِرْ لَكُمْ مِّن ذُنُوبِكُمْ﴾: *min* here is partitive (*lil-tab'īḍ*), meaning that He will forgive you what you did of sins before you submit, because Islam erases what came before it (*yajubbu mā qablahu*). These two views are weak in meaning, and the first is the correct one, because the partitive sense is appropriate here.

﴿وَيُؤَخِّرْكُمْ إِلَىٰ أَجَلٍ مُّسَمًّى﴾: The apparent meaning of this requires that if they do what they were commanded, they will be delayed until a specified term, and if they do not do it, they will not be delayed. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 71, verse 7–9:

﴿I called them so that You might forgive them﴾ That is, I called them so that they would believe and You would forgive them. He mentioned forgiveness, which is the consequence of faith, in order to show the ugliness of their turning away from it, for they turned away from their own happiness. ﴿They put their fingers in their ears﴾ They did this so that they would not hear his words. It is possible that they did this literally, or it may be an expression for the extreme of their turning away, as if they had done so. ﴿And they covered themselves with their garments﴾ That is, they made them a covering over themselves so that they would not hear his words, or so that he would not see them. It is possible that they did this literally, or it may be an expression of their turning away. ﴿And they persisted﴾ That is, they continued in their disbelief. ﴿Then I called them openly﴾ The grammatical analysis of "openly" (jihaaran, جهاراً) is that it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) derived from the meaning of the verb, like your saying "qa'ada al-qurfusa" (he sat in the crouching position), or it is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun whose estimated form is "da'a jihaaran" (he called openly), or it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning "mujaahiran" (openly, publicly). ﴿Then indeed I proclaimed to them and I spoke to them secretly, in secret﴾ He first mentioned that he called them by night and by day, then he mentioned that he called them openly, then he mentioned that he combined open calling and private calling, and this is the utmost of earnestness in advising and conveying the message (ﷺ). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Al-jihaad (open striving) is their being called in assemblies and places of gathering, and al-israar (secret calling) is calling each one individually."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 71, verse 11:

﴿He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain﴾. (mid'rar) is an intensive form derived from al-durr (الدر), which means an abundance of water. The verse is evidence that seeking forgiveness (istighfar) brings down rain. For this reason, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab went out to seek rain (istisqa'), and he did no more than seek forgiveness and then returned. He was asked: "We did not see you seek rain?" He replied: "By God, I sought rain with the most eloquent seeking." Then the rain fell. A man complained to al-Hasan about drought, and he said to him: "Seek forgiveness from God."

﴿What is the matter with you that you do not hope for dignity from God?﴾ Here there are four interpretations. The first is that *waqar* means honoring and esteem, so the meaning is: What is the matter with you that you do not hope that God will honor you in the abode of His reward? Al-Zamakhshari said this. On this reading, *Lillah* (for God) explains who is doing the honoring. Had it been placed later, it would have been an attribute of *waqaran* (dignity).

The second is that *waqar* means deliberateness and steadiness. The meaning is: What is the matter with you that you do not hope for God with deliberateness, remaining composed until you are able to reflect with your dignity? On this reading, *Lillah* is a direct object (*maf'ul*) to which the particle *lam* has been attached, like your saying *darabtu li-Zayd* (I struck for Zayd). The grammatical status of *waqaran* here is a verbal noun (*masdar*) in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), describing the manner of the action.

The third is that *al-raja'* (hope) here means fear, and *waqar* means greatness and sovereignty. The meaning is: What is the matter with you that you do not fear the greatness and sovereignty of God? On this reading, *Lillah* is, in meaning, an attribute of *al-waqar*.

The fourth is that *al-raja'* means fear, and *waqar* means settledness, from your saying *waqara bi-l-makan* (he settled in the place) when he remained in it. The meaning is: What is the matter with you that you do not fear being settled in the abode of permanence, whether in Paradise or in the Fire?

﴿And He has created you in stages.﴾ That is, stage after stage: man was a drop of semen, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, and so on through the rest of his states. It has also been said that *al-atwar* means different kinds: people are of various kinds in their colors, characters, languages, and other things.

﴿In seven heavens, layered one above another.﴾ This is mentioned in *al-Mulk* [3].

﴿And made the moon therein a light.﴾ The moon is only in the lowest heaven, yet it is permissible to say *fihinna* (in them) because it is in one of them, so it is considered to be in all of them, just as you say "So-and-so is in al-Andalus" when he is in part of it. The moon is described as a light and the sun as a lamp (*siraj*) because the light of a lamp is stronger than mere light: the lamp is what gives off illumination by which one sees, whereas light may be weaker than that.

The meaning is: What is the matter with you that you do not hope for God with deliberateness, remaining composed until you are able to reflect with your dignity? On this reading, *Lillah* is a direct object (*maf'ul*) to which the particle *lam* has been attached, like your saying *darabtu li-Zayd* (I struck for Zayd). The grammatical status of *waqaran* here is a verbal noun (*masdar*) in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), describing the manner of the action.

The third is that *al-raja'* (hope) here means fear, and *waqar* means greatness and sovereignty. The meaning is: What is the matter with you that you do not fear the greatness and sovereignty of God? On this reading, *Lillah* is, in meaning, an attribute of *al-waqar*.

The fourth is that *al-raja'* means fear, and *waqar* means settledness, from your saying *waqara bi-l-makan* (he settled in the place) when he remained in it. The meaning is: What is the matter with you that you do not fear being settled in the abode of permanence, whether in Paradise or in the Fire?

﴿And He has created you in stages.﴾ That is, stage after stage: man was a drop of semen, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, and so on through the rest of his states. It has also been said that *al-atwar* means different kinds: people are of various kinds in their colors, characters, languages, and other things.

﴿In seven heavens, layered one above another.﴾ This is mentioned in *al-Mulk* [3].

﴿And made the moon therein a light.﴾ The moon is only in the lowest heaven, yet it is permissible to say *fihinna* (in them) because it is in one of them, so it is considered to be in all of them, just as you say "So-and-so is in al-Andalus" when he is in part of it. The moon is described as a light and the sun as a lamp (*siraj*) because the light of a lamp is stronger than mere light: the lamp is what gives off illumination by which one sees, whereas light may be weaker than that.

The first is that *waqar* means honoring and esteem, so the meaning is: What is the matter with you that you do not hope that God will honor you in the abode of His reward? Al-Zamakhshari said this. ﴿And God has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth.﴾ This is an expression for their creation from the dust of the earth. "Nabatan" (نَبَاتاً) is a verbal noun (masdar) that comes in a form other than the usual masdar, or its implied sense is: "He caused you to grow, so you grew, a growing." It may also be in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). ﴿Then He will return you into it.﴾ That is, by resurrection from the graves. ﴿And God has made the earth for you a spread-out expanse.﴾ He likened the earth to a carpet (bisat) in its extension and in people's settling upon it. Some scholars derived from the word "bisat" that the earth is flat, not spherical, contrary to the view of the people of "al-ta'dil" (those who held that the earth is balanced and spherical). But there is room for scrutiny in this. ﴿Roads, wide paths.﴾ This was mentioned in al-Anbiya' [21:31]. ﴿And they followed those whom their wealth and children increased only in loss.﴾ That is, they followed their wealthy ones and their elders. It is also read as "waladuhu" (وَلدُه) with two fathas and as "wuld" (وُلْد) with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam; both have the same meaning. ﴿And they schemed a tremendous scheme.﴾ "Kubbar" (كُبَّار) with the shadda is more intensive than "kibar" (كِبَار) without it, and "kibar" without the shadda is more intensive than "kabir" (كَبِير).

Allah says: ﴿And they said, "Do not abandon your gods."﴾ That is, some of them enjoined one another to do so.

﴿Nor abandon Wadd or Suwa'.﴾ These are the names of their idols, which the people of Noah used to worship. It is related that they were the names of righteous men who lived in the early part of the world. When they died, the people of that age made images of them out of stone and said: "We look at them so that we remember their good deeds." That generation perished, and those who came after them magnified these images more and more, until they worshipped them besides Allah. Then these same idols passed on, in their very forms, to the tribes of the Arabs. It is also said that only the names passed on. Wadd belonged to the tribe of Kalb at Dumat al-Jandal, Suwa' belonged to Hudhayl, Yaghuth belonged to Murad, Ya'uq belonged to Hamdan, and Nasr belonged to Dhu al-Kala' of Himyar. Wadd is also read as وَدأ with a fatḥa on the wāw and as وُدّاً with a ḍamma on it, and these are two dialectal forms.

﴿And they have led many astray.﴾ The pronoun refers to the leaders of Noah's people. The meaning is that they led many of their followers astray. This is part of Noah's speech, peace be upon him, and so is ﴿and do not increase the wrongdoers except in error﴾, which is a supplication against them. Al-Zamakhshari said that it is coordinated with the statement ﴿"My Lord, they have disobeyed me"﴾ [Nuh: 21], and the sense is: he said, "My Lord, they have disobeyed me," and he said, "Do not increase the wrongdoers except in error."

﴿Because of their sins they were drowned﴾. This is a statement from Allah, informing about their situation. The word ما here is a redundant particle (ma za'ida) used for emphasis. The prepositional phrase has been placed first, also for emphasis, to make clear that their drowning and their entry into the Fire were caused by their sins, which are disbelief and all other acts of disobedience.

﴿And they were made to enter a Fire﴾, meaning Hell. The past tense is used because the matter is certain. It is also said that the intended meaning is that they were exposed to the Fire, and this exposure is expressed by the word "made to enter."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 71, verse 26:

﴿And Noah said: "My Lord, leave not upon the earth any dweller from among the disbelievers."﴾ Diyaran (ديّاراً) is one of the words used in general negation. It is said: "ma fi al-dar diyar" (ما في الدار ديار), meaning there is no one in the house. Its pattern is fiy'al (فيعال), and its original form was diywar (ديوار), in which the waw was changed to a ya' and then assimilated into the ya'. Its pattern is not fi'al (فعال), because if it were, it would have been said dawwar (دوار), since it is derived from al-dawr (الدور) or from al-dar (الدار). It has been related that Noah, peace be upon him, did not make this supplication against his people until he had despaired of their faith, and after God had brought forth from their loins every believer.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 71, verse 28:

﴿My Lord, forgive me and my parents﴾. From this it is derived that the sunnah in supplication is that a person should put his own supplication for himself before his supplication for others. Noah's parents were believers, peace be upon him. Ibn 'Abbas said: Noah had no disbelieving father; between him and Adam, peace be upon them both, there were no such fathers. The name of Noah's father was Lamak ibn Mutawshalakh, and his mother was Shamkha bint Anush, as related by al-Zamakhshari. ﴿And whoever enters my house as a believer﴾. It was said: his house is the mosque. It was also said: the ship. And it was said: his law (shari'ah), which he called a house by way of metaphor; but this is far-fetched. And it was said: his dwelling, and this is more likely, because it is the literal meaning. ﴿And for the believing men and the believing women﴾. This is a supplication for forgiveness for every believing man and believing woman in general. It is also evidence for the permissibility of this, contrary to those later scholars who said that it is not permissible to supplicate for forgiveness [for others]. And it is evidence for the permissibility of this, contrary to those later scholars who said that it is not permissible to supplicate for forgiveness for all believers in general; this is an error and a narrowing of God's vast mercy. Some scholars said: the God who answered Noah, peace be upon him, so that by his supplication He drowned all the disbelieving people of the earth, is worthy of answering him so that by his supplication He shows mercy to all believing men and women. ﴿Destruction (tabaran)﴾: that is, perdition. And God knows best.
